- When sentiment is strongly negative (e.g., < -0.4), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid excessive sell-off bias.  
- When sentiment is strongly positive (e.g., > 0.3), model often overreacts upward; cap upward momentum or reduce slope to prevent overshoot.  
- Model consistently underestimates true price in early 30-day horizon when sentiment is neutral or mildly negative — increase baseline by 1–2% in such cases.  
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior period), model frequently overreacts with continued steep rise; apply mean reversion bias to dampen momentum.  
- If sentiment history shows repeated short-term reversals (e.g., alternating +/–), model tends to lag in adjusting — add 1–2 days of lagged sentiment weight to forecast.  
- In low-volatility periods (e.g., sentiment flat or near-zero), model often underestimates mean reversion — increase forecast variance slightly to reflect hidden volatility.
